About holy #Liturgy in the #EOTC

👉Question: When the other three Eastern Orthodox churches have three liturgies, why do we have fourteen liturgies?

👉Answer: This is a matter of faith. We know that the liturgy is a very sacred and mysterious act, and these fourteen liturgies are named after the saints who have been entrusted with the secrets of the Holy Spirit. They participated in the composition of the liturgy, each contributing their own genius.

The Ethiopian Orthodox Church has a unique liturgical tradition that includes fourteen different Anaphoras (the part of the Eucharistic Prayer in which the bread and wine are consecrated). These Anaphoras are attributed to different saints and church fathers who contributed to the development of the church's theology and liturgy.

The fourteen Anaphoras used in the Ethiopian Orthodox Church are: St. Basil, St. Gregory, St. Cyril, St. Dioscorus, St. John the Evangelist, St. James, St. Adai and Mari, St. Julius, St. Philoxenus, St. Peter, St. Matthew, St. Mark, St. Luke, and St. Menas. Each of these saints represents a unique theological perspective, and their contributions are recognized and celebrated in the Ethiopian Orthodox Church through the use of their respective Anaphoras.

The use of multiple Anaphoras in the Ethiopian Orthodox Church is based on the belief that each saint has a unique contribution to make to the understanding of the Eucharist. It is believed that the Holy Spirit inspired each of these saints to write their Anaphoras, and that each one offers a different perspective on the mystery of the Eucharist and its significance in the life of the church.

The Ethiopian Orthodox Church also recognizes the three Anaphoras used by other Eastern Orthodox churches, namely the Anaphoras of St. John Chrysostom, St. Basil, and the Presanctified Gifts. However, the church believes that the use of multiple Anaphoras allows for a deeper understanding of the Eucharist and a more complete expression of the church's theology.

The liturgy they composed was inspired by the Holy Spirit and met the required standards. It was not simply put together by a person or a committee who collected money and then released it. When we consider the mystical composition of our these liturgies, it is truly wonderful. There is no word of God that is not included or touched upon. Why should we limit ourselves to only three liturgies, as in the case of the other Eastern Orthodox churches? They have their own reasons for having only these three liturgies in their canon.

To finish,, the Ethiopian Orthodox Church has fourteen different Anaphoras that are used during Mass, each attributed to a different saint or church father who contributed to the development of the church's theology and liturgy. The use of multiple Anaphoras allows for a more complete expression of the church's theology and a deeper understanding of the mystery of the Eucharist.

Question: How can I overcome my anxiety? How can I find peace in the midst of life's trials?

Answer: Are we, as Orthodox Christians, meant to worry? Our Lord and Savior, Jesus Christ, told us not to worry, so why are we worried? When a person is separated from God, sin becomes their dwelling place. Sin and lack of understanding deprives us from peace and makes us anxious.

A person without God has no peace or sleep. In general, a person who is dwelling in sin loses everything, and is filled with anxiety. Therefore, we are told not to worry and to "Cast all your worries on God, for He cares for you" (1 Peter 5:7).

In the sixth chapter of the Gospel of Matthew, it is written, "And why do you worry about clothes? See how the flowers of the field grow. They do not labor or spin. Yet I tell you that not even Solomon in all his splendor was dressed like one of these. If that is how God clothes the grass of the field, which is here today and tomorrow is thrown into the fire, will He not much more clothe you—you of little faith? So do not worry, saying, ‘What shall we eat?’ or ‘What shall we drink?’ or ‘What shall we wear?’ For the pagans run after all these things, and your heavenly Father knows that you need them. But seek first His kingdom and His righteousness, and all these things will be given to you as well" (Matthew 6:28-33).

This is why Orthodox Christians say "Our Father" in prayer, asking God to "have mercy on us as a father has compassion on his children" (Psalm 103:13). In addition, in Psalm 102, verse 1, it is written, "Praise the Lord, my soul; all my inmost being, praise His holy name. Praise the Lord, my soul, and forget not all His benefits—who forgives all your sins and heals all your diseases, who redeems your life from the pit and crowns you with love and compassion, who satisfies your desires with good things so that your youth is renewed like the eagle’s."

If God has mercy on us and can fulfill our desires, why should we worry? Worrying and thinking are different. We can think, dream, and plan without worrying. Worry is the result of despair, but we are people who have hope.

If we have everything we need with God, why should we give up? Our purpose is to do what we can with God and never give up hope. If we fall into sin, we repent, for "the one who conceals their sins does not prosper, but the one who confesses and renounces them finds mercy" (Proverbs 28:13). If we are reconciled to God through repentance, what we lost will be returned to us. Therefore, we should not give up but rather think it through.

Let us give all our worries to God, focus on what is expected of us, and leave the rest to Him. As the apostles said, "Cast all your anxiety on Him because He cares for you" (1 Peter 5:7). We need to understand that we are required to do this.

Knowing that anxiety is the result of sin and a sign of separation from God, the solution is to live with God, repent of our sins, listen to God, and let go of things that worry us.

Peace can be found in the midst of life's trials when we live with God. Jesus Christ is the Prince of Peace, and in John 14:27, He said, "Peace I leave with you".

Question፦ What is the Ethiopian Orthodox Church Teaching on the Soul After Death?

Answer፦ The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church teaches that after death, the soul and body separate. The soul continues to exist in an abstract form, while the body is laid to rest in the grave. It is believed that both the wicked and the righteous will experience this separation, but their ultimate fate differs.

According to the Orthodox doctrine, those who have committed evil deeds will go to hell, while those who have done good deeds will go to heaven. The criteria for entering heaven are based on the teachings of Matthew chapter 25, where Jesus speaks of acts of kindness such as giving bread and drink to the needy. It is believed that the righteous, who have demonstrated virtuous behavior in their earthly lives, will be rewarded with eternal life in heaven.

The concept of the afterlife in the kingdom of heaven is described as a state free from hunger, thirst, fatigue, envy, and racism. It is a realm where worldly limitations and transient nature cease to exist. The Church teaches that this eternal life is obtained through the resurrection, and it emphasizes that believers will not die but will be transformed.

The example of Christ's resurrection serves as a model for believers. Jesus, after being buried and guarded by soldiers, rose without the need for someone to open the grave or release Him. Similarly, the Church teaches that believers will be resurrected by the authority of Jesus Christ. It is believed that regardless of the circumstances of death, whether through burial or non-burial, all individuals will ultimately rise again when Christ returns.

The teaching of St. Paul provides further insight into the understanding of resurrection. He used the analogy of planting seeds to illustrate that just as grains sown in various conditions will ultimately grow, so too will individuals rise in accordance with their deeds. The wicked will rise with their sinful deeds, while the righteous will rise with their righteous deeds.

In summary, the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church affirms the existence of life after death. It teaches that the soul and body separate at the time of death, and while the body is laid to rest in the grave, the soul continues to exist. The ultimate fate of individuals is determined by their actions in life, with the wicked facing hell and the righteous attaining eternal life in heaven. The Church emphasizes the importance of resurrection, drawing inspiration from the example of Christ's resurrection, and teaches that believers will be transformed and enter into a state free from worldly limitations in the kingdom of heaven.

What is the basic purpose of #marriage? Is there a difference between secular marriage and a marriage conducted in church?

✍️Answer፦ The institution of marriage holds a deep significance in the Orthodox Church, reflecting the union of the bridegroom and the bride. It is regarded as a sacred mystery that is celebrated through a ceremony conducted in the church, accompanied by a sacrament that symbolizes the joining and oneness of the couple. In the words of Scripture, "A man shall leave his father and mother and be joined to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh" (Matthew 19:5). Thus, marriage is a profound mystery in which the couple commits to love and cherish each other exclusively, with the intention of starting a family, sharing their lives and possessions, and living together as long as God permits.

The purpose of marriage can be understood through three pillars: mutual support, procreation, and safeguarding against adultery. Firstly, marriage provides a framework for helping and supporting one another. Recognizing the words of God, "It is not good for man to be alone. Let us create a suitable helper for him" (Genesis 2:18), Orthodox teachings emphasize that marriage is a divine gift that assists individuals on their spiritual journey. At its core, marriage relies on genuine affection and love between spouses, where both partners prioritize the needs of their spouse, care for each other, and honor God through their commitment.

Secondly, marriage is seen as a means of continuing the generations and fulfilling the commandment to multiply. After blessing Adam and Eve in Paradise, God instructed them to "multiply and fill the earth and subdue it..." (Genesis 1:28). This divine blessing signifies God's approval of marriage and the union of Adam and Eve. In the Orthodox tradition, God's presence is invoked during the marriage ceremony, just as He was present during the union of Adam and Eve in Paradise. This demonstrates the significance of a legal marriage, solemnized in the holy church where Christ's body and blood are offered.

Lastly, marriage serves as a safeguard against the temptations of adultery. As the Apostle Paul advised, "Because of the temptation to sexual immorality, each man should have his own wife and each woman her own husband" (1 Corinthians 7:2). By committing to a holy marriage, individuals avoid the perils of yielding to lustful desires outside the confines of a sacred bond. It is essential for those living a religious life to steer clear of adultery, and marriage provides a path to resist such temptations.

Thus, the primary goal of marriage is to walk together in righteousness, pursuing eternal life and inheriting the Kingdom of Heaven. Married life is understood as a spiritual journey, necessitating the initiation of the marriage covenant within the Christian framework of the Church. This sacramental aspect signifies the involvement of three parties: the couple and God. Without all three, a marriage cannot be considered complete. In the sacrament of marriage, the physical union of the couple mirrors the unity of Christ's body and the Church. As stated in the Holy Scriptures, "They will become one flesh" (Mark 10:8), the great mystery of physical and spiritual unity finds its fulfillment in the Holy Eucharist.

The reason for elevating marriage to the status of a sacrament within the Church lies in allowing the Lord Jesus Christ to be the head and center of the couple's spiritual journey. In the words of St. Paul, "This mystery is profound, and I am saying that it refers to Christ and the Church" (Ephesians 5:32). The sacramental aspect signifies the union between the divine and the physical, and it is through the visible service and the reception of invisible grace that this union is made possible. The Holy Communion, in particular, transforms the marriage into a new reality, where the couple becomes one flesh.

(Continues) 👇

In contrast, a secular marriage lacks the spiritual dimensions present in a sacramental marriage. In a secular system, the union may be regarded solely as a legal contract, devoid of the sacredness and blessings that come with celebrating Christ's presence. The profound mystery of the bridegroom and bride becoming one is not fully realized, so the couple misses out on the blessings and grace that could have been received through the sacramental marriage.

However, acknowledging that "My people are destroyed for lack of knowledge" (Hosea 4:6), those who unknowingly or knowingly entered into a secular marriage can repent and seek unity in the Holy Communion, commencing a righteous journey for the remainder of their days.

In summary, the purpose of marriage encompasses mutual support, procreation, and protection against adultery. The sacramental nature of marriage, conducted within the Church, signifies the union of the bridegroom and bride, mirroring the unity of Christ and the Church. The sacramental marriage, where the couple and God are active participants, enables the Lord Jesus Christ to be the focal point of their spiritual journey. In contrast, secular marriages lack the spiritual dimensions present in sacramental marriages and miss out on the blessings and grace bestowed upon couples who enter into a holy union.

👉 Question፦ Hello Father, I had a question. It is about the verse of the bible that says "love your enemy". How can we love people who are trying to destroy us? 

Answer፦ Indeed, the question you pose is of great significance, dear member. "Love your enemy," a principle taught by Christ, is often difficult to comprehend, especially when our enemies appear to bring us harm or destruction. The tenet seemingly contradicts our natural instincts of self-preservation and justice. As followers of the Orthodox faith, how then do we interpret this seemingly paradoxical instruction?

The Gospel according to Matthew, chapter 5, verse 44 tells us, "But I say to you, love your enemies, bless those who curse you, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who spitefully use you and persecute you." But who exactly are these enemies that we are called to love? Surely, it is not a call to love those who aim to obliterate our faith, subvert our rights, and bring calamity upon us.

In our Orthodox belief, our true enemy is not of flesh and blood, but the devil himself. The enemy that Christ instructs us to love is not one who seeks to eradicate our faith, usurp our lands, or eradicate our presence on earth. No, it is not a call for passive submission to destructive forces.

Instead, the enemies referred to here are those among our own brothers and sisters in faith with whom we might have disputes or disagreements, those who have perhaps hurt us or wronged us in personal or communal contexts. It is these individuals, who are nevertheless our brethren in faith, that we are instructed to love and forgive.

But when it comes to those who threaten our existence, our faith, and our lands, the Bible offers other wisdom. In these cases, we are called upon to stand firm, to defend our faith and our people. The Biblical figures such as the Prophet David, who defeated Goliath, and the Prophet Moses, who stood against the Pharaoh's tyranny, exemplify this righteous resistance. It is not sinful to stand against destructive forces, indeed it is a calling of duty to protect and preserve the sanctity of life, faith, and community.

So when we interpret the command to "love your enemies," it is essential to discern the context. It means to love and forgive those who share our faith and our common humanity, even when they wrong us in minor ways. It does not imply love for those who aim to destroy our religion, our church, our country, or our lives.

Our duty extends to correction too. If a member of our Orthodox faith engages in wrongful acts, it is our responsibility to gently and lovingly correct them, making them aware of their transgressions. To oppose an evil act is not hatred but a form of love, for it aims to help the individual correct their path.

Moreover, we ought to appreciate that we are called to love even those who do not share our faith, yet are united with us in patriotism, in common goodwill for humanity, and in the fight against destructive forces. Yet, we must not tolerate those who wish to disrupt peace, alter our faith, or destruct our nation. Our forefathers have demonstrated this through their actions.

For instance, during the Adwa war, our ancestors did not stand idle in the face of forces aiming to change our religion and destroy our nation. They did not misconstrue "love your enemy" to mean passive acceptance of such atrocities. Instead, they acted righteously, defended their faith and their land, and handed down to us a heritage of steadfastness and spiritual courage.

In the same way, may God grant us wisdom to discern between our enemies and those merely disguised as such. May He give us strength to love those whom we are called to love and the courage to stand against those who threaten to disrupt our faith and peace. May we walk in His ways, loving when we must love, and resisting when we must resist, until we reach our ultimate salvation.

May God bless us all.

Question፦ On 1 Tim 3:2 it says :"A bishop then must be blameless, the husband of one wife, vigilant, sober, of good behavior, given to hospitality, apt to teach" who are metropolitan bishops in Orthodox Church? Can they get married or can a bishop be a married person?

Answer፦ The nature of the ecclesiastical order as outlined in the Pauline epistle to Timothy gives us insight into the role of bishops within the Orthodox Church. The bishops, serving as successors to the apostles, are regarded as the principal teachers, administrators, and ceremonial leaders of the Church. In Orthodox tradition, bishops have always been seen as leading lives of celibacy, dedicating their lives entirely to the service of the Church and the will of God. This is manifested in their choice to live as monks, separated from worldly affairs from a young age.

From a historical perspective, we see that the apostles themselves had different backgrounds, including marital status and occupations. The focus, however, has always been on their role as disseminators of God's teachings. Similarly, the roles within the Church, be it bishops, priests, or deacons, have expanded and adapted with the growth of the Church, a point that is well illustrated in the example of the appointment of the first seven deacons, led by St. Stephen.

Now, it's important to understand that the evolution of roles within the Church does not imply a shift away from the principles established by St. Paul. Rather, it signifies the Church's efforts to faithfully fulfill its spiritual obligations as its reach expands. Hence, it is indeed the monks who have embraced a life of celibacy and full devotion to God that take up the mantle of the bishopric. This is consistent with the canons of the Orthodox Church.

While the Orthodox Church encourages celibacy for bishops, it also acknowledges the apostolic guidance for bishops to be 'the husband of one wife.' This underlines the significance of monogamy, but it should not be misconstrued as an injunction for bishops to be married. In the practical and historical context of the Church, the role of the bishop has been fulfilled by those who have embraced a monastic life of celibacy.

Yet, it's important to mention that the authenticity of the ecclesiastical office cannot be guaranteed by monastic life alone. It also requires a deep and genuine spiritual life and knowledge, the absence of which has unfortunately led to errors and aberrations. The Church, in its wisdom, acknowledges that all humans, including its leaders, are prone to mistakes and temptations, as seen in the account of Simon the Magician in the book of Acts. It is essential, then, to avoid appointing those lacking in spiritual knowledge and life to leadership positions in the Church.

And so our dear member, we find that the Church continues to adapt to the needs of its faithful while remaining anchored to its apostolic foundations. It understands the challenges of living a life of peace and equality but insists on this aspiration, urging its flock to transcend the earthly trials and tribulations in pursuit of God's will. Let us, therefore, remember to bear our responsibilities faithfully, both within the Church and in the wider world, and to uphold the principles of peace, equality, and righteousness as taught by the apostles and preserved by the saints. Amen.

As we know from the teachings of our Lord Jesus Christ in Matthew 12:39, he condemned the adulterous and wayward generation, hinting at a spiritual restlessness and discontent that undergirds the act of adultery itself.

This adulterous attitude stretches beyond mere romantic relationships and seeps into every aspect of life.

Adultery, then, is the act of desiring more than what is given to us by God. It is the refusal to accept and be content with what we have, to honour and cherish what God has bestowed upon us. It is a revolt against the divine will and order, which dictates that a man is meant for one woman and vice versa.

If we are prone to seeking the new and untried, we must strive to remain content with what we have, adhering to the teachings of God. Recognizing the harm and destructiveness of adultery is the first step towards redemption. This harm can manifest itself in various ways, whether it is through consuming inappropriate media, participating in illicit activities, or allowing our thoughts to wander into immoral territories.

The antidote lies in understanding the gravity of the sin and recognizing its consequences. Question፦ Can a pregnant women confess/repent? I ask that because it may be hard for her to do the prostrations that the priests usually ask us to do.

Answer፦ Answering from an Orthodox perspective, it is important to bear in mind the overarching emphasis our Church places on love, mercy, and the sanctity of human life. Pregnancy is a time of unique grace and responsibility, carrying and nurturing within oneself a life created in the divine image. It is a period where women should receive exceptional care, guidance, and protection. 

Now, as to the question of repentance during pregnancy, we must remember that God's forgiveness is not confined by physical gestures or actions, such as prostrations. Rather, true repentance begins in the heart and mind. When a person feels genuine remorse for their sins and seeks God's mercy, the journey towards reconciliation with the divine begins. Prostrations, kneeling, fasting, and the like are valuable aids on this journey, but they are not its essence. The essence is contrition and a sincere desire to turn away from sinful patterns. Thus, pregnant women, as well as all others who for one reason or another cannot perform certain acts of penance, can fully partake in the sacrament of confession and receive absolution for their sins.

If there exists any particular sin that the woman feels particularly burdened by during her pregnancy, it should not remain unspoken out of fear of physical restrictions. Our faith holds life and its preservation as paramount, and it does not demand that a pregnant woman risk her health or that of her unborn child to perform certain acts of penance. What is required is the sincerity of the heart and the genuine intention to rectify one's ways, rather than any physical demonstration of penitence.

Moreover, if any transgressions were committed before the woman discovered her pregnancy, she should bring them to light post-delivery. In the interim period, she should seek the counsel of wise and pious elders, stay constant in prayer, and try to lead a righteous life, nurturing the life within her with love and care. God, who is the ultimate source of wisdom and mercy, knows our intentions, our fears, and our struggles. 

While it is true that Orthodox canon permits certain exemptions for pregnant and nursing women, such as being excused from fasting or performing strenuous acts of prayer, it does not exclude them from spiritual engagement entirely. They are encouraged to maintain a strong prayer life and remain connected with their spiritual fathers for guidance and support.

Lastly, regarding a pregnant woman's participation in communal prayer, the Church recommends a balanced approach. While it's true that faith, not the quantity of prayers or their location, is the ultimate path to salvation, the Church also acknowledges the benefit of community and mutual prayer. A pregnant woman may pray at home, and if she chooses to partake in communal prayer, she should do so in a manner that does not compromise her health or wellbeing. After giving birth, the Church community should extend its arms in love and care, ensuring that the mother and child are enveloped in spiritual blessings and God's grace.

In sum, the Orthodox Church teaches us to prioritize the sanctity of life and the health of the mother and child during pregnancy. True repentance and reconciliation with God begins in the heart, and not in the physical acts associated with penance. While physical restrictions may prevent pregnant women from participating in some traditional acts of penance, they are not precluded from confessing their sins, seeking God's mercy, or participating in communal prayers in a manner that respects their physical condition.

Dear members of John's Repentance page, today is the monthly feast of St. George in the EOTC and so we send you this short writing for you to learn about the life of this great saint and martyr. 

St. George is a Christian saint who is widely known for his courage, steadfast faith, and unwavering devotion to God. He was born in 280 A.D. in the city of Capadocia, which was part of the Eastern Empire in Asia Minor. He came from a wealthy and noble Christian family and followed the usual career path of young nobleman by joining the Roman army.

St. George's ability and charm quickly brought him promotion within the army, and eventually, he was made a tribune or an officer in the Imperial Guard by the Emperor. According to one story, he was a friend of Constantine, another officer who later became the first Christian emperor. The legend says that St. George accompanied Constantine to Britain and visited some holy places, including Glastonbury and Caerleon. When he returned to Nicomedia, the capital of the Eastern Empire, he encountered the fierce storm of persecution against Christians.

Diocletian, the emperor at the time, issued a formal edict against Christians on February 23, 303 A.D., which was the feast of Termhlalia. The edict mandated that all churches should be leveled to the ground, all sacred books burned, all Christians who held any honorable rank were to be degraded and deprived of civil rights, and all Christians who were not officials were to be reduced to slavery.

Despite the persecution, St. George boldly stood up for his faith. He pushed his way through the market to read the proclamation in front of the awe-stricken crowd and then deliberately tore down the Imperial edict and threw it away. This act of defiance resulted in his arrest and subsequent encounter with Diocletian.

The Emperor tried to seduce St. George by promising him a higher position in the empire, but St. George remained steadfast in his faith. Diocletian then began to threaten him with unbearable tortures that he would inflict on him. St. George refused to renounce his faith, even in the face of torture, and eventually was imprisoned.

St. George's chastity and suffering are two prominent aspects of his story. Diocletian arranged for a very beautiful woman to spend the night with him in prison to try to debauch him. St. George, who could only look forward to heavenly joy, began to pray and within a short while managed to swing her heart to the Christian faith. She seriously began to inquire about salvation, and by morning she declared that she found her true Bridegroom, Jesus Christ. With great courage, she announced her Christianity to the Emperor and his men and joined the other saintly martyrs.

(Continues)👇🏾

As for his suffering, the tortures that were applied to St. George are too numerous to mention in depth, but it is worth noting his utmost love for Christ. His body was torn by a special instrument that had metallic teeth, and our Lord Jesus rose him after his death, leading to the conversion of many pagans. He was put in active lime, and water was poured on it. Again the Lord returned him back to life. The Emperor became very agitated, imagining that the Saint was using magic. He called his top magician, Athanasius, and requested him to prepare a lethal poison to kill St. George.
The Saint signed over the cup with the sign of the cross before drinking it, and of course, no harm came to him. The Emperor's counselors informed him that St. George's magic was, in fact, contained in the sign of the Cross itself. Another cup was also given to the Saint, but this time with his hands tied behind his back. The Saint signed it by his head, saying: "shall I drink it from here or here or here or here!!!"

As St. George stood before the emperor and his court, he was given one last chance to renounce his Christian faith and offer sacrifice to the idols. The emperor promised him great rewards, honors, and privileges if he would do so. But St. George refused, declaring that he would never deny his Lord and Savior Jesus Christ.

In a final act of defiance, the emperor ordered St. George to be beheaded. The saint willingly accepted his fate and went to his death with courage and grace. He is said to have uttered a prayer to God, thanking Him for the privilege of dying for the faith.

After his martyrdom, St. George's reputation as a courageous and holy man quickly spread throughout the Christian world. Churches were built in his honor, and his feast day was celebrated on April 23rd. He became known as the patron saint of soldiers, knights, and all who defend the faith.

Today, the legend of St. George and the dragon is still celebrated in many cultures around the world. It has become a symbol of strength, courage, and the triumph of good over evil. The story of St. George reminds us that even in the face of persecution and adversity, we can remain steadfast in our faith and trust in God's love and mercy.

Dear members of John's Repentance page, today is the monthly feast of St. George in the EOTC and so we send you this short writing for you to learn about the life of this great saint and martyr. As you read to partake from the blessing of the day, think about how you can incorporate your learnings to your personal life. 

St. George is a Christian saint who is widely known for his courage, steadfast faith, and unwavering devotion to God. He was born in 280 A.D. in the city of Capadocia, which was part of the Eastern Empire in Asia Minor. He came from a wealthy and noble Christian family and followed the usual career path of young nobleman by joining the Roman army.

St. George's ability and charm quickly brought him promotion within the army, and eventually, he was made a tribune or an officer in the Imperial Guard by the Emperor. According to one story, he was a friend of Constantine, another officer who later became the first Christian emperor. The legend says that St. George accompanied Constantine to Britain and visited some holy places, including Glastonbury and Caerleon. When he returned to Nicomedia, the capital of the Eastern Empire, he encountered the fierce storm of persecution against Christians.

Diocletian, the emperor at the time, issued a formal edict against Christians on February 23, 303 A.D., which was the feast of Termhlalia. The edict mandated that all churches should be leveled to the ground, all sacred books burned, all Christians who held any honorable rank were to be degraded and deprived of civil rights, and all Christians who were not officials were to be reduced to slavery.

Despite the persecution, St. George boldly stood up for his faith. He pushed his way through the market to read the proclamation in front of the awe-stricken crowd and then deliberately tore down the Imperial edict and threw it away. This act of defiance resulted in his arrest and subsequent encounter with Diocletian.

The Emperor tried to seduce St. George by promising him a higher position in the empire, but St. George remained steadfast in his faith. Diocletian then began to threaten him with unbearable tortures that he would inflict on him. St. George refused to renounce his faith, even in the face of torture, and eventually was imprisoned.

St. George's chastity and suffering are two prominent aspects of his story. Diocletian arranged for a very beautiful woman to spend the night with him in prison to try to debauch him. St. George, who could only look forward to heavenly joy, began to pray and within a short while managed to swing her heart to the Christian faith. She seriously began to inquire about salvation, and by morning she declared that she found her true Bridegroom, Jesus Christ. With great courage, she announced her Christianity to the Emperor and his men and joined the other saintly martyrs.

(Continues)👇🏾

As for his suffering, the tortures that were applied to St. George are too numerous to mention in depth, but it is worth noting his utmost love for Christ. His body was torn by a special instrument that had metallic teeth, and our Lord Jesus rose him after his death, leading to the conversion of many pagans. He was put in active lime, and water was poured on it. Again the Lord returned him back to life. The Emperor became very agitated, imagining that the Saint was using magic. He called his top magician, Athanasius, and requested him to prepare a lethal poison to kill St. George.
The Saint signed over the cup with the sign of the cross before drinking it, and of course, no harm came to him. The Emperor's counselors informed him that St. George's magic was, in fact, contained in the sign of the Cross itself. Another cup was also given to the Saint, but this time with his hands tied behind his back. The Saint signed it by his head, saying: "shall I drink it from here or here or here or here!!!"

As St. George stood before the emperor and his court, he was given one last chance to renounce his Christian faith and offer sacrifice to the idols. The emperor promised him great rewards, honors, and privileges if he would do so. But St. George refused, declaring that he would never deny his Lord and Savior Jesus Christ.

In a final act of defiance, the emperor ordered St. George to be beheaded. The saint willingly accepted his fate and went to his death with courage and grace. He is said to have uttered a prayer to God, thanking Him for the privilege of dying for the faith.

After his martyrdom, St. George's reputation as a courageous and holy man quickly spread throughout the Christian world. Churches were built in his honor, and his feast day was celebrated on April 23rd. He became known as the patron saint of soldiers, knights, and all who defend the faith.

Today, the legend of St. George and the dragon is still celebrated in many cultures around the world. It has become a symbol of strength, courage, and the triumph of good over evil. The story of St. George reminds us that even in the face of persecution and adversity, we can remain steadfast in our faith and trust in God's love and mercy.

Question: How can I overcome my anxiety? How can I find peace in the midst of life's trials?

Answer: Are we, as Orthodox Christians, meant to worry? Our Lord and Savior, Jesus Christ, told us not to worry, so why are we worried? When a person is separated from God, sin becomes their dwelling place. Sin and lack of understanding deprives us from peace and makes us anxious.

A person without God has no peace or sleep. In general, a person who is dwelling in sin loses everything, and is filled with anxiety. Therefore, we are told not to worry and to "Cast all your worries on God, for He cares for you" (1 Peter 5:7).

In the sixth chapter of the Gospel of Matthew, it is written, "And why do you worry about clothes? See how the flowers of the field grow. They do not labor or spin. Yet I tell you that not even Solomon in all his splendor was dressed like one of these. If that is how God clothes the grass of the field, which is here today and tomorrow is thrown into the fire, will He not much more clothe you—you of little faith? So do not worry, saying, ‘What shall we eat?’ or ‘What shall we drink?’ or ‘What shall we wear?’ For the pagans run after all these things, and your heavenly Father knows that you need them. But seek first His kingdom and His righteousness, and all these things will be given to you as well" (Matthew 6:28-33).

This is why Orthodox Christians say "Our Father" in prayer, asking God to "have mercy on us as a father has compassion on his children" (Psalm 103:13). In addition, in Psalm 102, verse 1, it is written, "Praise the Lord, my soul; all my inmost being, praise His holy name. Praise the Lord, my soul, and forget not all His benefits—who forgives all your sins and heals all your diseases, who redeems your life from the pit and crowns you with love and compassion, who satisfies your desires with good things so that your youth is renewed like the eagle’s."

If God has mercy on us and can fulfill our desires, why should we worry? Worrying and thinking are different. We can think, dream, and plan without worrying. Worry is the result of despair, but we are people who have hope.

If we have everything we need with God, why should we give up? Our purpose is to do what we can with God and never give up hope. If we fall into sin, we repent, for "the one who conceals their sins does not prosper, but the one who confesses and renounces them finds mercy" (Proverbs 28:13). If we are reconciled to God through repentance, what we lost will be returned to us. Therefore, we should not give up but rather think it through.

Let us give all our worries to God, focus on what is expected of us, and leave the rest to Him. As the apostles said, "Cast all your anxiety on Him because He cares for you" (1 Peter 5:7). We need to understand that we are required to do this.

Knowing that anxiety is the result of sin and a sign of separation from God, the solution is to live with God, repent of our sins, listen to God, and let go of things that worry us.

Peace can be found in the midst of life's trials when we live with God. Jesus Christ is the Prince of Peace, and in John 14:27, He said, "Peace I leave with you".

👉 Question፦ Why does God call Moses and Elijah apart from the prophets for his transfiguration on Mt. Tabor?

Answer፦ Indeed, the event on Mount Tabor, the Transfiguration of our Lord Jesus Christ, is one replete with divine mysteries and profound theological insights. The very essence of this event speaks volumes about the nature of Christ and His mission on Earth. Yet, the presence of Moses and Elijah alongside Christ is no mere happenstance. It carries with it a theological weight that must be understood in the light of both the Old and New Testaments.

Let us begin with Moses and Elijah: two towering figures in the narrative of God’s relationship with humanity. Moses, the lawgiver, conversed with the Almighty and brought forth the Ten Commandments from Sinai. His presence on Mount Tabor is an affirmation that Jesus is the fulfillment of the Law. In the book of Exodus, Moses, yearning to see the full glory of God, was told, “You cannot see my face, for no one can see me and live” (Exodus 33:20). Yet, on Mount Tabor, Moses stands beside the Incarnate God, witnessing His transfigured glory—a testament to the promises of God being fulfilled.

Elijah, on the other hand, represents the prophets. This fiery prophet, who was taken up into heaven in a whirlwind, represents the prophetic tradition that pointed towards the coming of the Messiah. His presence confirms Jesus as the long-awaited Messiah, the fulfillment of the prophetic utterances.

The presence of both Moses and Elijah beside Jesus serves as an irrefutable testimony to the Jews. They encompass the entirety of the Old Testament – the Law and the Prophets. Their presence proclaims that Jesus is neither a mere prophet nor just another wise teacher. He is the Messiah, the fulfillment of all that was promised.

Saint Peter’s exclamation, “Lord, it is good for us to be here,” is a testament to the profound realization of the divine mystery unfolding before them. The mountain, in its elevated state, is reminiscent of the Church, lifting us closer to the heavens and the divine. To reside in such a place, to dwell with God, is indeed the highest of all desires, echoing the sentiments of Prophet David in his psalm.

Moreover, when the masses stumbled at the teachings of Jesus, the apostles remained, for they recognized in Him the words of eternal life. The Transfiguration reaffirmed this belief, showing them a glimpse of the divine glory of Jesus, strengthening their faith in the face of impending trials.

To be in the presence of God, to witness His majesty and glory, is indeed the highest of all blessings. The Transfiguration serves as a beacon, a luminous event that calls us to recognize the true nature of Christ and to anchor our faith in Him. For in Him, the Law and the Prophets find their fulfillment, and in His light, we find our true purpose and calling.

The Meaning of Worthiness

Orthodox Faith: The person who approaches the Eucharist must be an Orthodox Christian having no doubt concerning the bread & wine being the true body and precious blood of Lord Jesus Christ.

Repentance & Confession: The person must be practicing the Sacrament of Repentance and Confession on regular basis as St. Paul said, “let a man examine himself” (1 Cor 11:28)

Reconciliation With Others: Lord Jesus Christ said, “If you bring your gift to the altar, and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar, and go your way. First be reconciled to your brother, and then come offer your gift” (Mt 5:23-24)

True Worthiness is Feeling Unworthy: St. Paul, the meek and humble apostle said, “I know nothing against myself, yet I am not justified by this” (1 Cor 4:4)

Obeying The Church Rules: concerning food abstinence before communion, physical cleanliness, and early attendance of the liturgy.

👉 The Eucharist as a Sacrifice

The Orthodox Church believes and confesses that the Eucharist is a sacrifice and an offering to God in addition to being a Sacrament. The following supports this belief:

The words of Lord Jesus Christ Himself, “This is My blood of the new covenant, which is shed for many” (Mt 26:28; Mk 14:24) – “This cup is the new covenant in My blood, which is shed for you” (Lk 22:20) – “This is My body which is broken for you” (1 Cor 11:24) – “This is My body which is given for you” (Lk 22:19). Undoubtedly, the terms “broken body” and “shed blood” refer to a sacrifice.

The presence of an altar in the Church confirms that the Eucharist is a sacrifice. St. Paul said, “We have an altar from which those who serve the tabernacle (Jews) have no right to eat” (Heb 13:10). Isaiah the Prophet said, “In that day there will be an altar to the Lord in the midst of the land of Egypt” (Is 19:19), this is a specific prophecy about the Coptic (Egyptian) Church which proves the presence of altars in the Christian era and consequently the presence of a sacrifice (the Eucharist).

Malachi the Prophet prophesied about the New Testament offering saying, “I have no pleasure in you, says the Lord of hosts, nor will I accept an offering from your hands. For from the rising of the sun even to its going down, My name shall be great among the Gentiles; In every place incense shall be offered to My name, and a pure offering; For My name shall be great among the nations, says the Lord of hosts” (Mal 1:10-11). This “pure offering” is nothing but the Eucharistic offering that Christians offer on their altars, for at which point in history did the Gentiles “in every place” offer an offering to the Lord?

St. Paul said, “Observe Israel after the flesh: Are not those who eat of the sacrifices partakers of the altar? What am I saying then? That an idol is anything, or what is offered to idol is anything (else)? Rather, that the things which the Gentiles sacrifice they sacrifice to demons and not to God, and I do not want you to have fellowship with demons. You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons; you cannot partake of the Lord’s table and the table of demons” (1 Cor 10:18-21). The apostle is comparing the table (altar) of the Lord to the altar of the pagans upon which unacceptable demonic sacrifices were offered, which proves that the Eucharist that is offered on the Christian altar is indeed a sacrifice.

Source: ‘The Church Sacraments’ by Archdeacon Habib Guirgess.

Question፦ I wanted to ask, if we're adopted into the body of Christ during baptism, how are we still of the body if the members of Christ don't sin, but we as human sin? Is it because of God's mercy we are still considered members, making it a mystery?
And why do we take Holy Communion multiple times in our life? What separated the remission of sin in the Eucharist from that of baptism? Does it have any connection to healing the sick members of Christs' body (aka sinful humans)

Dear seeker of truth, your question has been asked by many throughout the ages. It's a testament to the profound mystery of our faith, a faith that both challenges and embraces the intellect.

In our faith, baptism is a divine sacrament, a sacred beginning where one is initiated into the fold of Christ. Through this rite, a soul becomes part of Christ, not in a figurative sense alone, but in a profound, mystical union. This individual, regardless of their age of initiation, be it the fortieth or the eightieth day of their life, is thereby grafted onto Christ. Like a branch attached to a divine vine, they draw life and purpose from Him.

Thus, when we proclaim ourselves as Christians, we declare our membership in Christ. We become part of His divine body, co-heirs to His kingdom, and participants in the divine mysteries. Each Christian is like a part of a body, with Christ as the head. We, the many, are brought into unity through Him, a unity that is signified and sealed in the sacrament of baptism.

Yet, as you rightly note, the reality of human sin stands in stark contrast to this divine ideal. But remember, while sin may mar our relationship with God, it doesn't sever our divine adoption granted at baptism. St. John reminds us that the children of God are distinguished from the children of the devil by their actions. When we sin, our transgressions do not arise from God but from our own fallen nature.

Despite our transgressions, God's mercy remains boundless. Only a full denial of God, a total renunciation of our baptismal vows, would sever this bond of divine adoption. Obeying The Church Rules: concerning food abstinence before communion, physical cleanliness, and early attendance of the liturgy.

👉 The Eucharist as a Sacrifice

The Orthodox Church believes and confesses that the Eucharist is a sacrifice and an offering to God in addition to being a Sacrament. The following supports this belief:

The words of Lord Jesus Christ Himself, “This is My blood of the new covenant, which is shed for many” (Mt 26:28; Mk 14:24) – “This cup is the new covenant in My blood, which is shed for you” (Lk 22:20) – “This is My body which is broken for you” (1 Cor 11:24) – “This is My body which is given for you” (Lk 22:19). Undoubtedly, the terms “broken body” and “shed blood” refer to a sacrifice.

The presence of an altar in the Church confirms that the Eucharist is a sacrifice. St. Paul said, “We have an altar from which those who serve the tabernacle (Jews) have no right to eat” (Heb 13:10). Isaiah the Prophet said, “In that day there will be an altar to the Lord in the midst of the land of Egypt” (Is 19:19), this is a specific prophecy about the Coptic (Egyptian) Church which proves the presence of altars in the Christian era and consequently the presence of a sacrifice (the Eucharist).

Malachi the Prophet prophesied about the New Testament offering saying, “I have no pleasure in you, says the Lord of hosts, nor will I accept an offering from your hands. For from the rising of the sun even to its going down, My name shall be great among the Gentiles; In every place incense shall be offered to My name, and a pure offering; For My name shall be great among the nations, says the Lord of hosts” (Mal 1:10-11). This “pure offering” is nothing but the Eucharistic offering that Christians offer on their altars, for at which point in history did the Gentiles “in every place” offer an offering to the Lord?

St. Paul said, “Observe Israel after the flesh: Are not those who eat of the sacrifices partakers of the altar? What am I saying then? That an idol is anything, or what is offered to idol is anything (else)? Rather, that the things which the Gentiles sacrifice they sacrifice to demons and not to God, and I do not want you to have fellowship with demons. You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons; you cannot partake of the Lord’s table and the table of demons” (1 Cor 10:18-21). The apostle is comparing the table (altar) of the Lord to the altar of the pagans upon which unacceptable demonic sacrifices were offered, which proves that the Eucharist that is offered on the Christian altar is indeed a sacrifice.

Question፦ Why do we say "turn to the east" during #Liturgy? 

Answer፦ In the observances of our Orthodox liturgy, the act of turning towards the east transcends mere ritualistic formality, embodying instead a profound theological and spiritual orientation that unites us, in both memory and hope, to the very essence of our faith. Let us delve deeply into this sacred tradition, that its significance might illuminate our hearts as the rising sun illuminates the world.

From time immemorial, the east has beckoned to the human spirit as the cradle of divine revelation and the harbinger of the new dawn. It is towards this sacred horizon that our churches are meticulously oriented, guiding our collective gaze towards the birthplace of salvation, where the narrative of redemption unfolds in the radiant light of God’s mercy.

The east, as the domicile of our primordial heritage, harks back to the very beginnings of mankind in the Garden of Eden, positioned in the east, according to ancient texts. This direction thus becomes a symbol of our origins and our ultimate destination, the heavenly realm promised to us. Each orientation towards the east during liturgy is a vivid remembrance of this promise, a gesture that embodies our yearning for re-entry into that lost paradise, now transformed through Christ’s salvific work into the hope of eternal life.

Moreover, the nativity of our Lord in the east serves as a testament to the dawn of God's mercy upon humanity. The Magi, guided by the celestial star, embarked on their eastward journey, a journey that each Christian symbolically undertakes during the liturgy. This star, emblematic of divine guidance, beckons us to follow in their footsteps, leading us to the manger where light eternal was born into the world. Thus, turning to the east is to remember the Incarnation, a pivotal moment when the Divine mingled with the human, illuminating our path with the promise of redemption.

The Virgin Mary, revered as the dawn heralding the Sun of Righteousness, embodies the east’s spiritual significance. Just as the sun dispels the darkness at dawn, so did the birth of Christ through Mary illuminate a world ensnared in sin's shadow. This symbolic association underscores her role in the divine economy of salvation, making our eastward turn a commemoration of her who is theotokos, the Mother of God, and the luminous portal through which the true Light came into the world.

The redemptive sacrifice of Christ, enacted in the east, further consecrates this direction in the Christian liturgical tradition. Jerusalem, the city of His passion, death, and resurrection, anchors our faith's historical and spiritual reality in the eastern landscape. In turning east, we thus commemorate the paschal mystery, the crux of our faith, where through His Cross and Resurrection, Christ triumphed over death, offering us the path to salvation.

Our ecclesiastical heritage, rooted in the eastern origins of Christianity, finds its expression in this liturgical orientation. The early Church, burgeoning forth from Jerusalem, disseminated the Gospel from this eastern heartland. In facing east, we thus align ourselves with the apostolic journey, tracing the Church’s growth from its nascent beginnings to its global expanse, a testament to the enduring and universal message of hope and salvation.

The liturgical invocation to "look to the east" is, therefore, a call to remembrance, to faith, and to hope. It is an invitation to contemplate the manifold ways in which God’s grace has been manifested from the east - through creation, through the Incarnation, through the saints and martyrs who have gone before us, and in the eschatological hope of Christ’s Second Coming from the east.

In this sacred act, we are not merely turning our bodies towards a geographical direction; we are orienting our souls towards the Light of the World, whose rising we eagerly await.

It is a gesture laden with eschatological significance, a physical and spiritual posture of readiness for the Day of the Lord, when the true Light will dawn in its fullness.

Thus, as we turn towards the east in our liturgical rites, let us do so with hearts aflame with love, minds illuminated by faith, and souls stirred by the hope of the Resurrection. In this sacred orientation, may we find the strength to traverse the wilderness of this world, guided by the Star of Bethlehem towards the heavenly Jerusalem, where Christ, the Sun of Righteousness, reigns eternally.

Blessed be God, the Mother of God, the Holy Cross, and all the saints, now and unto the ages of ages. Amen.

About the #Tabot

In the hallowed traditions of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, the concept of the Tabot holds a place of profound spiritual significance, echoing the eternal covenant between the Divine and His people. This sacred object, often a consecrated replica or tablet made of wood or stone, represents the Ark of the Covenant itself, a testament to the indwelling presence of God among His faithful. 

The Essence of the Tabot

The Tabot, in its most profound sense, is not merely a physical object but a tangible manifestation of God's glory, an altar upon which the divine presence rests. It is a symbol of the covenant, a bridge between the temporal and the eternal, signifying God's promise to dwell among His people. Just as the Ark of the Covenant was commanded to be built by God and served as the throne of His presence to the Israelites, the Tabot serves a parallel purpose in the Ethiopian Orthodox Church, embodying the living God's presence within the sanctuary.

Historical and Theological Foundations

The origins of the Tabot trace back to the ancient scriptural commandments given to Moses on Mount Sinai. Here, God instructed Moses to construct the Ark, a sacred container for the Tablets of Law, symbolizing God's covenant with Israel. This divine command illuminates the Ark's (and by extension, the Tabot's) role as a sacred depository of God's Word and His law, a physical embodiment of His eternal truths and promises.

In the Ethiopian Orthodox tradition, the Tabot is revered with utmost sanctity, mirroring the reverence the Ark received in the Old Testament. Each church houses a Tabot, consecrated and hidden from the public eye, symbolizing the Ark's historical and spiritual journey from Sinai to Zion, reflecting Ethiopia's deep connection to the biblical covenant.

Spiritual Significance and Worship

The worship and veneration of the Tabot are imbued with profound theological meaning. It is not the wood or stone that the faithful revere, but the divine presence it signifies. The Tabot, as the Ark before it, is a focal point of worship, drawing the faithful closer to the mysteries of the divine. In every liturgical celebration, the Tabot becomes the altar upon which the Holy Sacrifice is offered, linking the congregation with the heavenly liturgy and the communion of saints.

This sacred object reminds the faithful of God's promise to be with His people, to guide and protect them. It is a symbol of faith, a call to holiness, and a beacon of hope, signifying the eternal presence of God in His Church and among His people.

The Tabot in the Life of the Church

The presence of the Tabot in the Ethiopian Orthodox Church is a testament to the continuity of divine worship from the Old Covenant to the New. It is a witness to the Incarnation, the ultimate manifestation of God's presence among His people through Jesus Christ. The Tabot, therefore, not only connects the faithful to their ancient heritage but also to the living reality of Christ's sacrifice and resurrection.

In the annual rites and processions, the Tabot is carried with great pomp and reverence, encapsulating the journey of the Ark and symbolizing the movement of God's people towards the heavenly Jerusalem. These processions are not mere rituals but deeply spiritual events that invite reflection on the mystery of salvation and the journey of faith.

Conclusion: The Call to Holiness

The reverence for the Tabot in the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church is a call to remembrance, a reminder of God's eternal covenant with humanity, and an invitation to live in accordance with His divine law. It beckons the faithful to a life of holiness, urging them to embody the virtues of the Gospel in their lives.

The first Ananias we meet, alongside his wife Sapphira, is indeed the one who, having lied to the Holy Spirit about the proceeds from a sale of property, faced immediate death as a consequence of his actions (Acts 5:1-10). This event serves as a stern warning about the severity of deceit in the heart, especially in matters concerning the Holy Spirit. As it is written, "Be sure your sin will find you out" (Numbers 32:23).

The second Ananias, whom we encounter later in Acts, is a devout man in Damascus, known for his adherence to the Law and respected by all Jews in that region (Acts 22:12). It is this Ananias whom God calls to heal Saul (who becomes Paul) of his blindness, following Saul's dramatic encounter with Christ on the road to Damascus (Acts 9:10-18). This Ananias is an example of faithful obedience and courage, stepping into a situation that could have been perilous, given Saul's reputation at the time.

Thus, the confusion arises not from inconsistency in the narrative, but from the presence of two individuals sharing the same name, a common occurrence in scriptures and historical texts.

The lesson we draw from the Ananias in Damascus is profound: God calls us, often out of our comfort zone, to participate in His divine plan, to be instruments of His grace and healing. This term encapsulates our commitment to preserving the authentic teachings and traditions as handed down from Christ Himself to His Apostles and through them to the Church.

The use of "Orthodox" began in the early Christian era, particularly as a way to distinguish the Church that adhered faithfully to the teachings defined in the Ecumenical Councils from various heretical groups that had diverged from these established doctrines. It was crucial in times of doctrinal disputes to affirm the identity of the Church that remained faithful to the apostolic and patristic teachings. Hence, the term "Orthodox" became a definitive marker of the true Church that maintained fidelity to the Christian faith as it was universally recognized and proclaimed.

The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church embodies this commitment to orthodoxy, having received the Christian faith in the early Apostolic Age and nurtured it through centuries, steadfast amid various challenges. Our adherence to the term "Orthodox" is a testament to our dedication to uphold the true faith and practices as received from the generations of faithful who preceded us.

The word "Tewahedo" uniquely characterizes our Ethiopian Orthodox faith, signifying the unity of Christ's divine and human natures in one, without division or separation. This profound theological principle is intrinsic to our faith, shaping our worship, our spirituality, and our very identity as followers of Christ in the Ethiopian tradition.

Our Church, bearing the name Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, thus stands as a beacon of the undiluted Christian faith, embracing the unity of Christ and the apostolic teachings preserved and cherished in our tradition.

The Tefisihee Mariam, or the Praise of Mary, is a significant hymn chanted by deacons, lauding the Virgin Mary, the Theotokos, for her pivotal role in the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ. This hymn exemplifies our veneration of the Mother of God, not as a deity, but as the chosen vessel through whom God became man for our salvation. It embodies our acknowledgment of her virtues and her unique place in our salvation history.

The verse you're referring to "አንቲ ውእቱ መሶበ ወርቅ ንጹሕ እንተ ውስቴታ መና ኅቡዕ ኅብስት ዘወረደ አም ሰምያት ወሀቤ  ሕይወት ለኩኩ ዓለም," which translates to "Thou art the pot of pure gold wherein is hidden the manna, the bread which came down from heaven giving life unto all the world," beautifully articulates the Orthodox Christian belief in Mary as the Ark of the New Covenant. This verse draws us into the deep typology found in Scripture, where Mary is seen as fulfilling and surpassing the types and symbols of the Old Testament. Thus, the Tefisihee Mariam is not merely a hymn of praise but a profound theological affirmation of the Incarnation and the central role of the Virgin Mary in our salvation. They invite us to ponder the mystery of our salvation and the extraordinary role that Mary plays in it, encouraging us to seek her intercessions and to emulate her faith and obedience to God's will.

👉🏾 Question፦ Hey, I hope you are doing well. I have questions about the day of worship in the Ethiopian Orthodox Church.

I hope you can get back to me, and thank you so much for your time!

Answer፦ Peace be upon you, and may the grace of Our Lord be with you.  Your thoughtful questions demonstrate a yearning to understand the ancient paths of our faith. Let us delve into the sacred texts and traditions to illuminate this matter.

You are correct that the Lord commanded the Sabbath to be held sacred in the Old Testament (Exodus 20:8-11).  However, we must remember that with the coming of Christ, we are not merely under the Law, but under grace (Romans 6:14). 

The early Church, comprised of the Apostles and disciples who walked with Jesus, began to observe the first day of the week, Sunday, as the Lord's Day, in commemoration of His glorious Resurrection (John 20:1).  This shift did not negate the Sabbath; rather, it fulfilled its spiritual purpose in Christ.  

The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, in its ancient wisdom, upholds both the Sabbath and the Lord's Day. We observe the Sabbath on Saturday with prayers and scriptural readings, acknowledging its significance as a day of rest and reflection.  

However, we celebrate the Divine Liturgy, the Holy Eucharist, on Sunday, the Lord's Day, in joyous celebration of His victory over death.  This practice aligns with the teachings of the early Church Fathers and the traditions passed down through generations.

While some historical accounts attribute the prominence of Sunday worship to Emperor Constantine, it's crucial to remember that the Ethiopian Orthodox Church, in its isolation, maintained its apostolic traditions without Roman influence.  Our observance of Sunday as the primary day of liturgical celebration stems from our understanding of its significance in light of the Resurrection.

Your pursuit of understanding is commendable, my child.  Remember, the essence of our faith lies not merely in rigid adherence to specific days but in our heartfelt devotion to God.  May He continue to illuminate your path as you seek Him with sincerity and humility.  

If you have further questions, do not hesitate to ask.  May the blessings of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit be upon you.

Beloved brethren in Christ, those who seek the wisdom of the Church and the guidance of the Holy Scriptures, let us incline our hearts toward the sacred mystery of marriage, which is established by the hand of God Himself. For as the Lord, in His boundless love, formed Eve from Adam’s side, so too does He unite man and woman in a bond that is holy, immutable, and full of grace.

One Mind, One Heart, One Will

The life of a husband and wife is not one of discord but of unity. They are called to live with one mind, one heart, and a common will. Their steps must be guided by mutual counsel, and their hearts must beat in harmony, reflecting the perfect union found in Christ and His Church. As the Apostle teaches, “Wives, submit to your husbands as to the Lord. For the husband is the head of the wife, even as Christ is the head of the Church” (Ephesians 5:22-23). And likewise, “Husbands, love your wives as Christ loved the Church and gave Himself up for her” (Ephesians 5:25).

This is not a submission of servitude, nor a love that seeks dominion, but a harmony wherein each gives of themselves fully to the other. The wife’s obedience is one of trust and love, just as the Church submits to Christ, and the husband’s love is sacrificial, just as Christ laid down His life for His people.

A Covenant of Mutual Respect and Sacrifice

Marriage is a covenant wherein there is neither superiority nor inferiority, but a sacred bond where both husband and wife serve one another. The husband does not rule as a tyrant, nor does the wife exist as a subject, but rather, they are yoked together in Christ, bearing one another’s burdens with humility and grace. “A husband should give up his body for his wife, and a wife for her husband, to the point of suffering.” This is love: not in word only, but in deed and in truth.

Their love is to be an example to their children, a radiant light that teaches by action more than by words. They must walk in righteousness, both within their home and beyond its walls, so that their offspring may see the beauty of Christian life and follow in their footsteps.

The Divine Institution of Marriage

Marriage is not a mere human agreement but a divine institution. It is pure and undefiled, established from the very beginning by God Himself, who said, “It is not good for man to be alone; let us make for him a helper suitable for him” (Genesis 2:18). Thus, He created one man for one woman, and one woman for one man, binding them together in a union that is blessed and sanctified. To transgress this divine order by introducing another spouse is to defile the sanctity of marriage and to sin against God’s holy design.

On the day of their marriage, the husband and wife stand before God and swear an oath that neither sickness nor hardship, neither poverty nor affliction, shall separate them. Their love must not be fickle nor their commitment conditional, for “what God has joined together, let no man separate” (Mark 10:9). If they hold steadfast to this vow, their household will be built upon a firm foundation, unshaken by the tempests of life.

A marriage rooted in Christ does not falter at every trial, nor does it crumble under the weight of worldly burdens. Rather, it is fortified by the love that St. Paul describes: “Love is patient, love is kind. It does not envy, it does not boast, it is not proud. It does not dishonor others, it is not self-seeking, it is not easily angered, it keeps no record of wrongs. Love does not delight in evil but rejoices with the truth. It always protects, always trusts, always hopes, always perseveres” (1 Corinthians 13:4-7).

Love calls for patience in times of conflict, kindness in times of distress, and endurance when trials arise. A Christian couple does not hastily seek separation, nor do they harbor resentment, but rather, they seek understanding and reconciliation, just as Christ reconciled the Church unto Himself.

Marriage as a Fortress of Faith

A household built upon the Word of God stands firm against the storms of life. Our Lord has declared: “Everyone who hears these words of mine and puts them into practice is like a wise man who built his house on the rock. The rain came down, the streams rose, and the winds blew and beat against that house; yet it did not fall, because it had its foundation on the rock” (Matthew 7:24-25).

So too must a Christian marriage be built upon the unshakable foundation of God’s truth. A husband and wife who live by Scripture will find that their marriage is strengthened, their love deepened, and their trials overcome by the power of divine grace.

The Sacredness of the Marriage Bed

Marriage is honorable, and the marriage bed is undefiled. This is a sacred union, meant to be kept pure and holy. The body of the husband belongs to the wife, and the body of the wife belongs to the husband. To defile this bond through infidelity is a grievous sin, for it is a rejection of the trust and love that God has ordained between them. Let them remain faithful to one another, guarding their hearts from temptation and their eyes from wandering, for “the two shall become one flesh” (Mark 10:8).

🏽👉🏽👉🏽The Fasting of #Nineveh: A Lesson in Divine Mercy and Repentance

Beloved brethren in Christ, let us set our hearts upon the wisdom of the Holy Fathers and open our ears to the sacred teachings that have been passed down through generations. In contemplating the Fasting of Nineveh, we do not merely look upon an ancient event, but we witness the unchanging nature of God's mercy and justice, a lesson for all who have ears to hear and hearts to repent.

The Origin of the Fasting of Nineveh

In the sacred canons of our Holy Mother, the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, there are seven fasts ordained for the faithful. Among them, the Fasting of Nineveh holds a place of great significance, calling to mind the repentance of an entire city that turned away from its wickedness and sought the mercy of the Almighty. This fast is observed on the tenth day of the year, a time set apart for deep reflection, contrition, and the seeking of divine favor.

Nineveh: The Great City of Old

The city of Nineveh, a name written upon the pages of sacred history, was established by the mighty hunter Nimrod upon the banks of the Tigris River. This city, magnificent in its splendor and strong in its might, is described in the Scriptures as a place of great renown.

The walls of Nineveh stretched for twelve kilometers, encircling a city adorned with palaces, temples, and markets. It was the heart of the Assyrian Empire, much like Oslo, Addis Ababa, or Stockholm in our modern times—an imperial city that commanded the affairs of nations.

But let us not forget, brethren, that Nineveh was not only known for its greatness in power but also for its greatness in transgression. For the Assyrians, descendants of Shem’s son Asshur (Genesis 10:22), had walked the path of wickedness, and their sins had risen as a stench before the throne of God.

The Assyrian Empire and Its Fate

Nineveh stood as the jewel of the Assyrian Empire, a nation that reached the pinnacle of its strength and expanded its dominion far and wide. The empire, in its might, conquered the northern kingdom of Israel and later even took King Manasseh of Judah captive, leading him to Babylon. Yet, in the providence of God, Jerusalem was not utterly destroyed, for the Lord had set His name upon that holy city.

In the days of King Hezekiah, the Assyrians, in their pride, raised their hand against the people of God and provoked the Most High to wrath. The might of human armies is as dust before the breath of the Lord, and so it was that in a single night, the angel of the Lord struck down 185,000 Assyrian soldiers. The morning light revealed the truth—where there was once the clamor of a great army, now lay only the silence of death. (2 Kings 19:35)

Sennacherib, the proud king of Assyria, who had boasted against the living God, fled to his city of Nineveh, where his own sons would later strike him down, fulfilling the judgment of the Almighty.

Yet Nineveh, despite its strength and power, could not stand against the judgment of God. In the year 612 B.C., the city was captured and destroyed by the Babylonian Empire, its glory turned to dust, and its walls reduced to rubble. Thus did the mighty fall, and thus did the words of the prophets come to pass.

The Significance of the Fast

Beloved, why do we fast the Fast of Nineveh? Is it not to remember the mercy of God? Is it not to recall that no sin is too great to be forgiven when true repentance is found in the heart of man?

The people of Nineveh, though steeped in wickedness, humbled themselves before the Lord. When Jonah, the reluctant prophet, preached in their streets, they did not harden their hearts, but they tore their garments, put on sackcloth, and fasted, from the least to the greatest. Even the king rose from his throne, covered himself in ashes, and decreed a fast for all. And what did God do? In His infinite compassion, He turned away His wrath and spared them.

Thus, my brethren, the Fasting of Nineveh stands as a testament to the boundless mercy of our Lord. It is a call to every soul burdened by sin to repent, to seek the Lord while He may be found, and to humble oneself before His mighty hand. Let us not be as those who trust in their strength, nor as those who boast in their wisdom, for the Lord brings the mighty low and exalts the humble.

To Him be the glory, to the Virgin be honor, and to the Cross be eternal praise!

May the name of the Holy God be praised forever and ever in every tongue that He has created, today and always. 

May the blessings of God's mother, the virgin, and the cross be upon us.
Amen.

🏽👉🏽👉🏽#Marriage and #Attitude: A Christian Perspective

Beloved followers of the Orthodox teachings, may the grace and peace of our Lord be with you. Today, we reflect on an essential lesson—one that is foundational to a joyful and enduring marriage. The key to harmony between husband and wife is not found in wealth, status, or even outward gestures of love, but in the attitude they cultivate toward one another, toward life itself, and ultimately toward God.

The Power of Attitude in Marriage

Attitude is the unseen force that shapes the way a husband and wife see each other, the way they understand their roles, and how they respond to the trials that inevitably arise. A heart filled with gratitude and humility will make marriage a dwelling place of peace; a heart filled with pride and selfishness will turn it into a battlefield.

A husband who sees his wife as a partner given by God will cherish her with love and devotion, just as Christ loves His Church.

But if he regards her as a rival, a mere servant to his needs, his heart will grow hardened with pride, anger, and even hatred.


Likewise:

A wife who recognizes her husband as a blessing from the Lord, dedicating herself to loving him and their family with a sacrificial heart, will radiate warmth, support, and self-giving love.

But if she sees him as an oppressor, resentment will take root, growing into bitterness and, in time, into outright hostility.


Marriage is not simply a contract; it is a divine calling. When both husband and wife acknowledge this truth and see themselves as children of God, entrusted with carrying out His plan, their hearts will be drawn closer to Him and to each other. A home filled with such faith will be a place of refuge, a sanctuary of love, and a small church where Christ is honored.

The Consequence of a Materialistic Attitude

If a couple sets their hearts on money, possessions, and worldly gain, their attitude toward each other and their circumstances will be poisoned by selfishness and greed. Love will be replaced by rivalry, and instead of serving one another, they will begin to use each other. But if they see their marriage as a means to manifest God’s love—not only within their household but to all people—they will cultivate a spirit of service and generosity. Their home will become a dwelling place of God, where He is glorified through their love and hospitality.

The Role of Perspective in Overcoming Challenges

Every marriage will encounter challenges—this is inevitable. But what matters is how these challenges are faced. The thoughts, visions, and values that shape our perspective determine whether we find joy and fulfillment or sink into despair and frustration.

If a spouse carries a negative outlook, believing the worst in situations and in people, the solution is not to fight fire with fire.

Responding to negativity with more negativity is like pouring oil on flames. It does not resolve conflict but deepens it.


Instead, we are called to respond with patience, prayer, and a joyful heart. Do not allow yourself to be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good (Romans 12:21). This is not merely a command but a spiritual law: the one who retaliates with anger is not only harming their spouse but also losing their peace with God.

A Final Exhortation

To those who are married, and to those preparing for marriage, know this: your attitude is the soil in which your love will either flourish or wither. If you cultivate an attitude of gratitude, humility, and faith, your marriage will be a source of unshakable joy. If you allow pride, selfishness, and resentment to take root, no amount of external effort will save it.

Therefore, examine your hearts, shape your perspectives through prayer, and build your marriage upon the firm foundation of Christ. In doing so, you will not only experience peace in your own home but will reflect the love of God to the world.

Glory to God, the Ever-Born Virgin, and the Glorious Cross!

May the name of the Holy God be praised forever and ever in every tongue that He has created, today and always. 

May the blessings of God's mother, the virgin, and the cross be upon us.
Amen.
